name: Device Access Security
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Lock down console, vty and enable access with secrets and local users, set password policy and compare RADIUS with TACACS+.

lesson.intro: One login to a router or switch can reroute, sniff or shut down a network. This lesson builds device access control: line passwords, enable secret, password types, local users, privilege levels, login hardening, password policy, MFA and centralized AAA.
objectives: Protect console, vty and enable mode, and predict which password IOS asks for
Read password types 0, 5, 7, 8 and 9 and explain why type 7 is weak
Build a login baseline with local users, privilege levels, timeouts, SSH and banners
Describe password policy, MFA, certificates and biometrics
Compare the AAA functions and RADIUS with TACACS+, and read a method list

sections.title: Lines, modes and line passwords
sections.key: Each way into a device is a line (console, vty, aux), and a line password works only when the line has both `password` and `login`.
sections.body:
Unbox a new switch, plug in a console cable, and you are at a prompt with no password. Type `enable` and you control everything. Device access control closes those doors.

**User EXEC** (`R1>`) allows basic show commands. **Privileged EXEC** (`R1#`), reached with `enable`, allows everything. You protect the way into the device and, separately, the step up.

[[visual]]

The simplest protection is a shared **line password**: `password` sets it and `login` makes IOS ask for it. A password without `login` is never requested; `login` without a password refuses the connection.

[[code]]

visual.title: The ways in, and their defaults
rows: `login` but no password: refused with "Password required, but none set"
An auxiliary port on some routers
A back door: give it `login local`, or `no exec`

sections.code:
! Shared line passwords: simple, but everyone knows the same one
line console 0
 password C0nsole!Pass
 login
!
line vty 0 15
 password Vty!Pass2024
 login
sections.tip: Line passwords prove that someone knows the password, not who they are. The local usernames later in this lesson fix that.
sections.pitfall: Setting a console password and forgetting the login command. IOS stores the password but never prompts for it, so the console stays wide open.

check.question: A new router's vty lines show login but no password. What happens when someone tries to Telnet in?
choices: They reach user EXEC mode without a prompt
They reach privileged EXEC mode directly
The connection is refused with "Password required, but none set"
They are prompted for the enable secret instead
check.explanation: vty lines default to login with no password, so IOS has nothing to check and refuses the session. The console, by contrast, defaults to no login and lets users straight in.

sections.title: enable password versus enable secret
sections.key: `enable secret` stores a hash and `enable password` stores clear text; when both are configured, only the enable secret is accepted.
sections.body:
Two global commands protect the step from user EXEC to privileged EXEC. `enable password` stores the password in clear text. `enable secret` stores a one-way **hash**: IOS hashes what the user types and compares, so the clear text is never kept.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

You cannot view a secret, but you can overwrite it with `enable secret` again or remove it with `no enable secret`. In practice, configure only `enable secret` (IOS warns if you reuse its value for `enable password`). With neither command, SSH users reach privileged mode only through a `privilege 15` username.

visual.title: Which password does `enable` want?
rows: Only the enable secret works; the enable password is ignored
Straight into privileged mode, no password

sections.code:
R1# show running-config | include enable
enable secret 9 $9$nhEmQVczB7dqsO$X.HsgL6x1il0RxkOSSvyQYwucySCt7qFm4v7pqCxkKM
enable password Cisco123
! Typing enable now requires the secret; Cisco123 is ignored.
sections.pitfall: Treating enable password as a backup that works if the secret is forgotten. When both exist, only the secret is accepted, so the old password is dead weight that still leaks in clear text.

check.question: A router has both enable password Cisco123 and an enable secret configured. A user types enable and enters Cisco123. What happens?
choices: Access is granted, because either password works
Access is granted, because enable password is checked first
IOS asks for a username instead
Access is denied, because only the enable secret is accepted
check.explanation: When both commands exist, IOS checks only the enable secret. The enable password is ignored entirely.

sections.title: Password types: 0, 7, 5, 8 and 9
sections.key: The number before a stored password shows how IOS keeps it: 0 is clear text, 7 is reversible, and 5, 8 and 9 are one-way hashes.
sections.body:
Look at any running configuration and you will see a number in front of stored passwords. The CCNA expects you to read it.

[[visual]]

`service password-encryption` turns every would-be clear-text password (line passwords, `enable password`, `username ... password`) into type 7. That only stops someone glancing at a printout: free tools reverse it instantly. `no service password-encryption` decrypts nothing; existing passwords stay type 7 until changed.

A hash cannot be reversed. The only attack is guessing, hashing each guess and comparing, which types 8 and 9 make deliberately slow. Configuring the enable secret again with another algorithm replaces it.

[[code]]

visual.title: IOS password types
rows: Strongest; the default on some newer releases

sections.code:
R1(config)# enable algorithm-type scrypt secret Str0ng!Pass
R1(config)# service password-encryption
R1(config)# do show running-config | include secret|password
service password-encryption
enable secret 9 $9$nhEmQVczB7dqsO$X.HsgL6x1il0RxkOSSvyQYwucySCt7qFm4v7pqCxkKM
 password 7 070C285F4D06
sections.deeper:
**Type 4** appeared briefly in some IOS releases as a SHA-256 hash, but a coding flaw made it weaker than type 5 (no salt, a single fast iteration). Cisco replaced it with types 8 and 9; never use it.

**Which algorithm for usernames?** The same keywords work there: `username admin algorithm-type scrypt secret ...` stores a type 9 hash. `enable algorithm-type sha256 secret ...` gives type 8.
sections.pitfall: Believing service password-encryption makes passwords safe. Type 7 is obfuscation: anyone with a copy of the config can reverse it in seconds. Use secrets (types 5, 8, 9) wherever IOS offers them.

check.question: A configuration contains: password 7 070C285F4D06. What is true about this line password?
choices: It is an scrypt hash that cannot be reversed
It was hidden by service password-encryption and can be decoded easily
It is clear text that IOS displays with a 7 prefix
It can only be produced by the enable secret command
check.explanation: Type 7 is the weak reversible encryption applied by service password-encryption. Free tools turn 070C285F4D06 back into the original password, which is why secrets are preferred.

sections.title: Local usernames and login local
sections.key: Local usernames give each administrator their own login; `login local` on a line checks them, while plain `login` uses the shared line password.
sections.body:
With shared line passwords, the logs can only say "someone logged in." When a change breaks the network at 2 a.m., you want a name. A **local username database** gives every administrator their own credentials.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

SSH needs a username to authenticate, so vty lines that accept SSH need `login local` (or AAA). Even networks with a central AAA server keep one or two strong local accounts as the fallback for when the server is unreachable.

visual.title: Usernames and login local
rows: A user with a hashed password (type 5, 8 or 9)
The same, with a type 9 hash
The user lands in privileged EXEC, no `enable` needed
Legacy: clear text, or type 7. A username has a password or a secret, not both
Prompts for a username and password and checks the local database
Uses the line password and ignores your usernames

sections.code:
username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!Str0ng
username helpdesk secret H3lp!Desk2024
!
line console 0
 login local
!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh
sections.deeper: **When `password` is still needed.** A few older features, such as CHAP on serial links, must know the clear-text password, so they use `username ... password`. Avoid it everywhere else. One username has either a password or a secret, but different usernames in the same configuration can mix the two.
sections.tip: Review accounts with `show running-config | section username`. A secret shows as type 5, 8 or 9; a password shows as 0 or 7.
sections.pitfall: Typing `login` when you meant `login local`. The line then asks for the line password only, so SSH logins fail and your user accounts are silently ignored.

check.question: Which line subcommand makes IOS prompt for a username and password and check them against the usernames configured on the device?
choices: login
password local
login local
transport input ssh
check.explanation: login local uses the local username database. Plain login checks the line's shared password, and transport input only controls which protocols may connect.

sections.title: Privilege levels
sections.key: IOS privilege levels run from 0 to 15: level 1 is user EXEC, level 15 is privileged EXEC, and a session runs commands at its level and below.
sections.body:
Not every administrator should do everything. Every IOS command belongs to one of 16 **privilege levels**, and a session can run commands at its own level and every level below it.

[[visual]]

Three commands do the work. `username NAME privilege N secret ...` places a user at level N when they log in with `login local`. `privilege exec level N COMMAND` moves a command to level N. `enable secret level N ...` sets a password for `enable N`.

[[code]]

Every level from 2 to 15 shows `#`, so check with `show privilege`. Large networks usually do this job with TACACS+ command authorization instead.

visual.title: Privilege levels
rows: User EXEC: basic show commands, ping, traceroute. A plain login lands here
Empty until you move commands in: custom roles
Privileged EXEC, reached with `enable`: everything, including configuration

sections.code:
! Operations staff land at level 5 and may also clear counters
privilege exec level 5 clear counters
username ops privilege 5 algorithm-type scrypt secret 0ps!Team2024
!
R1> show privilege
Current privilege level is 1
R1> enable
Password:
R1# show privilege
Current privilege level is 15
sections.pitfall: Assuming the # prompt means full control. Every level from 2 to 15 shows #; run show privilege to see the real level.

check.question: A user logs in through login local with the account created by username ops privilege 5 secret 0ps!Team. Which commands can ops run?
choices: Only commands assigned to level 5
Commands at level 5 and at every level below it
Every command, because the prompt shows #
Only level 1 commands until ops types enable
check.explanation: A session can use the commands at its own level and all lower levels. Level 5 shows the # prompt like level 15, but configuration commands stay at level 15 and are not available.

sections.title: A hardened login baseline
sections.key: Harden logins with idle timeouts, SSH-only vty lines, an access-class ACL and a warning banner, and know the order in which banners appear.
sections.body:
Passwords are only part of the job. A few more commands close common gaps:

- `exec-timeout 5 0` logs out idle sessions after 5 minutes and 0 seconds. `exec-timeout 0 0` means never: fine in a lab, risky in production.
- `transport input ssh` on the vty lines blocks Telnet, which sends passwords in clear text.
- `access-class 10 in` on the vty lines lets only management subnets reach the login prompt.
- **Banners** warn users. Each starts and ends with a delimiter character, such as `#`.

[[visual]]

A login banner should say access is for authorized users only and is monitored. Never write "Welcome", and never reveal the model, software or location.

[[code]]

Verify with `show running-config | section line`, `show running-config | include secret|username` and `show users` (who is logged in, and idle time).
sections.code:
hostname R1
enable algorithm-type scrypt secret En@ble!Secret9
service password-encryption
username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!Str0ng
!
banner motd #
Authorized access only. All activity is logged and monitored.
#
!
line console 0
 login local
 exec-timeout 5 0
!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exec-timeout 10 0
 access-class 10 in
!
access-list 10 permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255
sections.tip: SSH on the vty lines also needs a hostname, `ip domain-name` and an RSA key, as covered in the SSH pack.
sections.pitfall: Leaving `exec-timeout 0 0` from lab work on a production device. Any session left open, on a console or a forgotten SSH window, stays logged in forever.

activity.title: Harden a router's logins
activity.prompt: Work through each lab check: protect enable mode with a secret, create a local user, make the console and vty lines use login local, add a timeout and a banner. After each step run show running-config and look at how IOS stored each password (the type number). Ask yourself which of them an attacker holding a copy of this config could read.

check.question: A user connects to the console of a router that has banner motd, banner login and banner exec configured, and logs in successfully. Which banner appears last?
choices: The exec banner
The MOTD banner
The login banner
None; only one banner can be shown per session
check.explanation: On a console or Telnet login, the MOTD banner shows first, then the login banner, then the credential prompts, and the exec banner appears only after a successful login.

sections.title: Password policy: complexity and management
sections.key: Password policy covers complexity (length matters most) and management (unique, changed, stored as hashes); IOS can enforce a minimum length and block repeated failures.
sections.body:
The blueprint lists password **complexity** and **management** as policy elements: the written rules every account follows.

**Complexity** makes guessing expensive. Length matters most, so a passphrase of four random words beats a short string of symbols. Policies also ban dictionary words, names, the company name and breached passwords, and usually require mixed character types.

**Management** covers a password's life:

- Change every default before a device goes live.
- One unique account per administrator, never a shared admin password.
- Never reuse a password across devices.
- Change it on any sign of compromise, when staff leave, and periodically.
- Keep only hashes on devices, and human copies in a password vault, not a spreadsheet.

IOS enforces some of this itself:

[[visual]]

visual.title: Policy in IOS
rows: Rejects new passwords shorter than 10 characters
After 5 failed logins within 60 seconds, refuses all logins for 120 seconds
Hosts permitted by this ACL can still log in during that quiet period, so attackers cannot lock admins out
A syslog message for every failed login (`login on-success log` for successes)

sections.tip: Current NIST guidance favors long passwords changed on evidence of compromise rather than on a fixed schedule; Cisco material still lists periodic changes.
sections.pitfall: Writing a policy so painful (short expiry, strange symbol rules) that people write passwords on sticky notes. A policy users cannot live with creates a new vulnerability.

check.question: Which single change to a password policy adds the most resistance to brute-force attacks?
choices: Requiring one symbol in every password
Raising the minimum length from 8 to 14 characters
Changing passwords every 30 days
Displaying a warning banner before login
check.explanation: Each added character multiplies the number of possible passwords, so length grows the search space far faster than adding one required symbol. Banners and expiry do not slow an attacker who already holds a hash.

sections.title: Beyond passwords: MFA, certificates and biometrics
sections.key: Multifactor authentication combines different categories (something you know, have or are); a password plus a security question is still only one category.
sections.body:
A password is **something you know**, and anything you know can be phished, guessed or reused. The alternatives add other kinds of proof.

[[visual]]

**Multifactor authentication (MFA)** needs factors from at least two different categories, so a stolen password alone fails.

**Digital certificates** are issued and signed by a trusted **certificate authority (CA)**. They expire, and can be **revoked** early (when an employee leaves, say), after which they fail. The matching private key never leaves the owner's device, so copying the certificate file is not enough.

**Biometrics** are convenient and hard to share, but cannot be changed if stolen, some readers are fooled by photos or molds, and injury or aging changes readings. So they are usually one factor among several.

visual.title: Authentication factors
rows: Private key on a laptop or smart card
Fingerprint, face, iris, retina, palm, voice
Password plus a push approval on a phone

sections.deeper: Routers and switches rarely do MFA themselves. The device hands the login to a central AAA server, which can demand the second factor (a challenge) before it accepts, as the next section shows.
sections.pitfall: Counting two passwords, or a password plus a security question, as two-factor authentication. Both are something you know; MFA needs different categories.

check.question: Which login method is true multifactor authentication?
choices: A password followed by a second password
A password followed by a security question
A password followed by a code from an authenticator app
A long passphrase with symbols
check.explanation: The app code proves something you have, and the password proves something you know: two different categories. The other options use only something you know.

sections.title: AAA: authentication, authorization and accounting
sections.key: AAA centralizes authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do) and accounting (what did you do) on a server such as Cisco ISE.
sections.body:
Local usernames work for ten devices. With two hundred, removing one administrator means touching every box, and the logs are scattered. **AAA** ("triple A") centralizes the job.

[[visual]]

The device the user connects to is the AAA client, called the **network access device (NAD)** or network access server (NAS). It collects the credentials and asks a central **AAA server**, such as Cisco **Identity Services Engine (ISE)**, which replies **accept**, **reject** or **challenge**.

[[visual 2]]

The same functions cover network access: a laptop authenticates with 802.1X, is authorized onto the staff VLAN, and accounting records how long it stayed.

visual.title: Three functions
rows: An engineer proves her identity with a password, certificate or MFA
She gets privilege 15, but may not run `reload` during business hours
What did you do, and when?
Every command she types is logged with her name and a timestamp

sections.pitfall: Mixing up authentication and authorization. Proving who you are is authentication; being allowed to run a command or join a VLAN after that is authorization.

check.question: An AAA server receives a correct password but still needs a one-time code from the user's phone before deciding. Which reply does it send to the network device?
choices: Accept
Reject
Challenge
Accounting start
check.explanation: A challenge asks for more information, which is how MFA works through AAA. Accept would admit the user on the password alone, and reject would deny access.

sections.title: RADIUS, TACACS+ and IOS method lists
sections.key: TACACS+ (TCP 49, full encryption, per-command authorization) suits admin logins; RADIUS (UDP 1812 and 1813, only the password encrypted) suits network access.
sections.body:
Two protocols carry AAA between the device and the server:

[[visual]]

On IOS, `aaa new-model` turns AAA on. Logins then follow **method lists**, and with no default list, vty logins check local usernames, so create a local user first or you can lock yourself out.

`aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local` asks the TACACS+ servers first, and checks local usernames only if no server answers. A **reject** from a server is final.

[[code]]

`aaa authorization exec` lets the server set the privilege level; `aaa accounting commands 15` reports every level 15 command.

visual.title: RADIUS and TACACS+
rows: Authentication and authorization combined; accounting separate

sections.code:
username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!Str0ng
aaa new-model
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.10.99.20
 key T@cKey!2024
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group tacacs+
sections.tip: Memory hook: TACACS+ has a T for TCP and for total encryption; RADIUS is the UDP one that hides only the password.
sections.pitfall: Expecting the local fallback to kick in when the AAA server rejects a password. The next method in the list is tried only when the server does not answer; a reject from the server is final.

check.question: Which protocol uses TCP port 49, encrypts the entire packet body and can authorize each command separately?
choices: RADIUS
TACACS+
SNMPv3
LDAP
check.explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, encrypts the full body and separates authentication, authorization and accounting. RADIUS uses UDP 1812 and 1813 and encrypts only the password.

keyTerms.definition: The R1# mode reached with the enable command (privilege level 15), where every command, including configuration, is available.
Global command that protects privileged mode with a one-way hash; it overrides enable password when both exist.
Global command that converts clear-text passwords to type 7, a weak reversible encryption.
A password hidden with Cisco's reversible algorithm; free tools decode it instantly.
A password stored as an scrypt hash, set with algorithm-type scrypt; the strongest option in IOS.
Line subcommand that authenticates users against the device's local username database instead of a line password.
One of 16 levels (0 to 15) that decide which commands a session may run; 1 is user EXEC and 15 is privileged EXEC.
Line subcommand that disconnects a session after a period of inactivity; 0 0 disables the timeout.
Message of the day banner shown to users when they connect; used for legal warnings.
Global command that refuses all logins for a quiet period after too many failures within a time window.
Authentication that requires factors from two or more categories: something you know, have or are.
A CA-signed, time-limited, revocable credential tied to a private key that proves identity.
Authentication (who you are), authorization (what you may do) and accounting (what you did).
Network access device: the router, switch, WLC or firewall acting as the AAA client between the user and the AAA server.
Open-standard AAA protocol on UDP 1812 and 1813 that encrypts only the password; used for network access such as 802.1X.
Cisco-developed AAA protocol on TCP 49 that encrypts the whole body and separates all three AAA functions; used for device administration.
An ordered list of AAA sources, such as group tacacs+ then local; the next source is tried only if the previous one does not answer.

summary: A line password needs both password and login; when both enable commands exist, only the secret works.
Type 0 is clear text and type 7 is reversible; 5, 8 and 9 are hashes, with 8 and 9 the strong choices.
login local checks per-person usernames and SSH needs it; level 1 is user EXEC and level 15 is enable mode.
Harden with exec-timeout, SSH only, an access-class ACL, legal banners and login block-for.
MFA mixes categories; certificates can be revoked; biometrics cannot be changed.
TACACS+ (TCP 49) for admins, RADIUS (UDP 1812, 1813) for network access; fallback only when no server answers.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new network technician how a Cisco router decides which password to ask for when someone connects to the console, connects over SSH and types enable, why type 7 passwords are not really secret, and how privilege levels and a TACACS+ server let you give the help desk read-only access. Finish by explaining when you would pick RADIUS instead.

questions.question: Which IOS lines carry Telnet and SSH sessions to a router?
choices: line console 0
line aux 0
line tty 1
line vty 0 4
questions.explanation: Remote sessions use virtual terminal (vty) lines. The console and aux lines are physical ports on the device.

questions.question: A technician plugs into the console of a switch with the configuration below. What happens?
questions.code:
SW1# show running-config | section line con 0
line con 0
 password C0nsole!Pass
 logging synchronous
choices: The switch prompts for C0nsole!Pass before allowing access
The technician reaches user EXEC mode without any password prompt
The console is disabled until login is added
The switch prompts for a username and password
questions.explanation: Without the login subcommand, IOS never asks for the line password, so the console is open. Adding login makes IOS prompt for C0nsole!Pass.

questions.question: An engineer telnets to a new router and sees the output below. What is the cause?
questions.code:
C:\> telnet 10.1.1.1
Password required, but none set

Connection to host lost.
choices: The router has no enable secret configured
transport input ssh is blocking Telnet
The vty lines have login configured but no password
An access-class on the vty lines denied the engineer's address
questions.explanation: vty lines default to login with no password, and IOS refuses the session with exactly this message. A missing enable secret only matters later, when the user types enable.

questions.question: A router has both enable password and enable secret configured with different values. Which value must a user enter after typing enable?
choices: The enable secret value
The enable password value
Either value
The console line password
questions.explanation: When both are configured, IOS uses only the enable secret and ignores the enable password.

questions.question: A router has neither enable password nor enable secret configured. An administrator logs in over SSH and types enable. What happens?
questions.code:
R1> enable
% No password set
R1>
choices: The administrator enters privileged mode with no prompt
IOS prompts for the vty password instead
IOS asks the administrator to create an enable secret
Access to privileged mode is refused
questions.explanation: With no enable password or secret, remote users cannot reach privileged mode at all and see "% No password set". Only console users are let in without a password in that case.

questions.question: Type the global configuration command that protects privileged mode with a hashed password of Gr8Secret! (use the plain form, without choosing an algorithm).
questions.explanation: enable secret stores a hash of the password rather than the clear text. Avoid enable password, which stores clear text.

questions.question: Match each IOS password type number to how the password is stored.

pairs.right: Weak reversible encryption from service password-encryption

questions.explanation: Types 0 and 7 can be read or reversed; 5, 8 and 9 are one-way hashes, with 8 and 9 designed to be slow to crack.

questions.question: A switch's configuration contains the lines below. An attacker obtains a copy of it. What can the attacker most easily learn?
questions.code:
service password-encryption
enable secret 9 $9$nhEmQVczB7dqsO$X.HsgL6x1il0RxkOSSvyQYwucySCt7qFm4v7pqCxkKM
!
line vty 0 15
 password 7 070C285F4D06
 login
choices: The enable secret, because type 9 is reversible
Nothing, because both passwords are hashed
The vty password, because type 7 can be decoded instantly
Both passwords, because service password-encryption covers the secret too
questions.explanation: The type 7 vty password decodes with free tools. The type 9 enable secret is an scrypt hash that would have to be cracked by guessing, which is slow.

questions.question: An engineer enables service password-encryption, then later enters no service password-encryption. What happens to the line passwords that were encrypted?
choices: They are decrypted back to clear text immediately
They stay type 7 until each password is changed
They are deleted from the configuration
They are converted to type 5 hashes
questions.explanation: Turning the service off only stops future encryption. Existing type 7 passwords remain encrypted until someone sets them again, at which point the new value is stored in clear text.

questions.question: Type the global command that encrypts all clear-text passwords in the configuration as type 7.
questions.explanation: service password-encryption converts line passwords, enable password and username password entries to type 7. It is weak, but better than clear text on a printout.

questions.question: Which three are changed by service password-encryption? (Choose three.)
choices: The console line password
The enable password
A username configured with the password keyword
The enable secret
A username configured with the secret keyword
questions.explanation: service password-encryption only touches passwords that would otherwise be clear text. Secrets are already stored as hashes, so they are left alone.

questions.question: Which command stores the enable password as a type 9 hash?
choices: enable algorithm-type sha256 secret Str0ng!Pass
enable password 9 Str0ng!Pass
enable algorithm-type scrypt secret Str0ng!Pass
service password-encryption 9
questions.explanation: algorithm-type scrypt produces type 9. algorithm-type sha256 produces type 8, and enable password never creates a hash.

questions.question: You are in line vty 0 15 configuration mode. Type the command that makes the lines authenticate users against the local username database.
questions.explanation: login local prompts for a username and password and checks the local database. Plain login would use the shared line password.

questions.question: With the configuration below, Telnet users are asked only for a password, and SSH logins fail. Which change fixes both problems?
questions.code:
username netadmin secret N3tAdm!n
!
line vty 0 4
 password Vty!2024
 login
 transport input telnet ssh
choices: Replace login with login local under the vty lines
Add service password-encryption
Change transport input to ssh only
Add enable secret N3tAdm!n
questions.explanation: login uses the shared line password and ignores the username database, and SSH needs username authentication. login local fixes both. Restricting transport to SSH would block Telnet but SSH would still fail.

questions.question: Why is username admin secret X preferred over username admin password X?
choices: secret allows the user to skip the enable password
secret stores a one-way hash instead of clear text or reversible type 7
secret is the only form that works with the console line
secret automatically gives the user privilege level 15
questions.explanation: The secret keyword hashes the password (type 5, 8 or 9). The password keyword stores clear text, or type 7 with service password-encryption. Privilege level is a separate option.

questions.question: A user connects to a router's console that has all three banners configured. Put what the user sees in order.
questions.explanation: MOTD comes first, then the login banner, then the credential prompts. The exec banner appears only after a successful login.

questions.question: You are in line console 0 configuration mode. Type the command that disconnects the session after 5 minutes and 0 seconds of inactivity.
questions.explanation: exec-timeout takes minutes and then optional seconds. exec-timeout 0 0 would disable the timeout entirely.

questions.question: What does exec-timeout 0 0 do on a line?
choices: Disconnects the session immediately
Disables the line
Uses the timeout set on the vty lines instead
Disables the inactivity timeout, so sessions never time out
questions.explanation: Zero minutes and zero seconds means no timeout at all. That is handy in a lab and risky in production.

questions.question: Which MOTD banner text follows best practice?
choices: Welcome to the HQ core router! Please log in.
Authorized access only. All activity is logged and monitored.
Cisco 4331, IOS XE 17.3, Building 2 basement.
Default login is admin, ask IT for the password.
questions.explanation: A banner should warn that access is restricted and monitored. "Welcome" sounds like an invitation, and model, software or location details help attackers.

questions.question: Security policy says credentials must never cross the network in clear text. Which line of this configuration breaks the policy?
questions.code:
enable algorithm-type scrypt secret En@ble!9
username admin algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!9
!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input telnet
 exec-timeout 10 0
choices: login local, because it sends the username unencrypted
exec-timeout 10 0, because it reveals session length
transport input telnet, because Telnet sends passwords in clear text
algorithm-type scrypt, because scrypt is reversible
questions.explanation: Telnet carries everything, including the typed password, unencrypted. transport input ssh is the fix. The scrypt secrets and login local are good choices.

questions.question: What does the command below do?
choices: After 5 failed logins within 60 seconds, the device refuses all logins for 120 seconds
Users may log in at most 5 times per 120 seconds
Sessions time out after 120 seconds of inactivity
The account that failed 5 times is deleted after 60 seconds
questions.explanation: login block-for enters a quiet period after too many failures in a window. It cripples online password guessing, though it cannot stop offline cracking of a stolen config.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes IOS reject any new password shorter than 12 characters.
questions.explanation: security passwords min-length enforces a minimum length for passwords configured after the command is entered.

questions.question: Which two are good password management practices for network devices? (Choose two.)
choices: Give every administrator a unique account instead of one shared admin password
Change every default password before a device goes into production
Use the same strong password on every device so it is easy to remember
Keep a spreadsheet of device passwords on a shared drive
Never change a password once it is strong enough
questions.explanation: Unique accounts give accountability and contain damage, and defaults are the first thing attackers try. Reusing one password, storing passwords in a shared file, or never rotating them all widen the blast radius of one leak.

questions.question: A fingerprint reader is an example of which authentication factor?
choices: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are
Somewhere you are
questions.explanation: Biometrics such as fingerprints, faces and irises are something you are.

questions.question: An employee leaves the company, and the CA revokes the certificate on her laptop. What happens if she tries to authenticate with it the next day?
choices: Authentication succeeds until the certificate's expiry date
Authentication succeeds because she still has the private key
Authentication is rejected because the certificate is revoked
The certificate is automatically renewed for 30 days
questions.explanation: Revocation ends a certificate's validity before its expiry date. Services that trust the CA check revocation and refuse the certificate even though she still holds the file and key.

questions.question: Match each credential to its authentication factor category.
questions.explanation: MFA combines categories. A hardware key or smart card is something you have; a face or fingerprint is something you are.

questions.question: Match each AAA function to the question it answers.

pairs.right: What are you allowed to do?
What did you do, and when?

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies identity, authorization grants permissions, and accounting records activity for auditing and billing.

questions.question: Which UDP port does a modern RADIUS server use for authentication requests?
questions.explanation: RADIUS uses UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting. Older servers used 1645 and 1646.

questions.question: Which three statements describe TACACS+? (Choose three.)
choices: It uses TCP port 49
It encrypts the entire body of each packet
It separates authentication, authorization and accounting, allowing per-command authorization
It uses UDP ports 1812 and 1813
It combines authentication and authorization in one response
It is the protocol 802.1X uses to reach the authentication server
questions.explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, encrypts the full body and keeps the AAA functions separate. UDP 1812/1813, combined authentication and authorization, and 802.1X all describe RADIUS.

questions.question: R1 has the configuration below. The TACACS+ server at 10.10.99.20 is powered off. What happens when admin tries to log in over SSH with a valid local username and secret?
questions.code:
aaa new-model
!
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.10.99.20
 key T@cKey!2024
!
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
!
username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!9
choices: The login fails, because TACACS+ is listed first
R1 tries the TACACS+ server, gets no answer, then authenticates admin against the local database
R1 skips authentication entirely until the server returns
R1 uses the enable secret instead of the username
questions.explanation: The method list tries group tacacs+ first; when no server responds, IOS moves to the next method, local. If the server had answered with a reject, the login would fail without trying local.

questions.question: A company wants employees' laptops to authenticate to the wired and wireless network with 802.1X. Which protocol will the switches and WLC most likely use to reach the authentication server?
choices: TACACS+
RADIUS
SNMP
Syslog
questions.explanation: 802.1X network access uses RADIUS between the authenticator (switch or WLC) and the server. TACACS+ is mainly used for administrators logging in to devices.

questions.question: Why do organizations use a central AAA server instead of local usernames on every device?
questions.answer: One central database means accounts are added, changed and removed in one place for every device, policies such as per-command authorization and MFA are applied consistently, and accounting records of who did what are collected centrally. Local accounts are kept only as a fallback.
questions.explanation: Local usernames do not scale: with hundreds of devices, removing one administrator would mean editing every configuration, and logs would be scattered.

questions.question: Which privilege levels correspond to user EXEC mode and privileged EXEC mode on a Cisco router?
choices: 0 and 1
1 and 15
1 and 7
15 and 16
questions.explanation: User EXEC (R1>) is level 1 and privileged EXEC (R1#), reached with enable, is level 15. Levels 2 to 14 are available for custom roles, and there is no level 16.

questions.question: Type the global command that creates a local user named noc at privilege level 5 with the secret N0c!View (use the plain secret form, without choosing an algorithm).
questions.explanation: privilege 5 sets the level the user lands at after a login local login, and secret stores a hash of the password rather than the password itself.

questions.question: R1 has the configuration below. User noc logs in over SSH. Which statement is true?
questions.code:
privilege exec level 5 clear counters
username noc privilege 5 algorithm-type scrypt secret N0c!View
!
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh
choices: noc starts at level 1 and must type enable 5 first
noc starts at level 5 and can run clear counters plus all level 0 and 1 commands, but cannot enter configuration mode
noc has full access because the prompt shows #
noc can run clear counters and nothing else
questions.explanation: The username's privilege 5 places noc at level 5 after login local. A session can use commands at its level and below, so clear counters (moved to level 5) and the normal level 1 commands work, while configure terminal stays at level 15.

questions.question: Type the EXEC command that displays the privilege level of your current session.
questions.explanation: show privilege prints a line such as Current privilege level is 15. It is the reliable check, because every level from 2 to 15 shows the same # prompt.

questions.question: An administrator connects with SSH version 2 to a router that has banner login, banner motd and banner exec configured. Put what she sees in order.
questions.explanation: Over SSH the login banner is shown before authentication, and the MOTD banner only after a successful login, followed by the exec banner. On the console and Telnet, MOTD comes first.

questions.question: Policy requires per-user accountability and encrypted remote sessions. Based on the output, which two changes are needed on these lines? (Choose two.)
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | section line vty
line vty 0 4
 password 7 0822455D0A16
 login
 transport input all
choices: Replace login with login local and create local usernames
Change transport input all to transport input ssh
Add service password-encryption
Add exec-timeout 0 0
Add a banner motd
questions.explanation: login checks one shared line password, so nobody can tell who logged in; login local with personal usernames fixes that. transport input all allows Telnet, which sends credentials in clear text. The password is already type 7, and the other options do not meet either requirement.

questions.question: Repeated guessing triggers login block-for and R1 enters its quiet period. How can administrators on 10.10.99.0/24 still log in during that time?
choices: Configure login quiet-mode access-class with an ACL that permits 10.10.99.0/24
Configure exec-timeout 0 0 on the vty lines
Replace enable secret with enable password
Nothing; quiet mode blocks every source
questions.explanation: login quiet-mode access-class names the hosts that remain allowed while the router refuses everyone else, so an attacker cannot lock the administrators out. Timeouts and enable passwords have nothing to do with quiet mode.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes IOS write a syslog message for every failed login attempt.
questions.explanation: login on-failure log records each failure, so a guessing attack shows up in the logs. login on-success log does the same for successful logins.

questions.question: Which weakness is specific to biometric credentials such as fingerprints?
choices: They are as easy to share with coworkers as passwords
They cannot be changed if the biometric data is stolen, and some readers can be fooled by photos or molds
They expire on a fixed date like certificates
They only work with RADIUS servers
questions.explanation: You can change a password or revoke a certificate, but not your fingerprint. Spoofing with photos or molds and changes from injury or aging are why biometrics are usually one factor among several.

questions.question: A security audit requires a record of every configuration command each administrator entered, with timestamps. Which AAA function provides it?
choices: Authentication
Authorization
Accounting
Encryption
questions.explanation: Accounting records what users did and when. Authentication proved who they were, and authorization decided which commands they were allowed to run.

questions.question: Match each AAA server reply to what it tells the network device.

pairs.right: The credentials are valid; let the user in
The credentials are wrong; deny access
More information is needed, such as an MFA code

questions.explanation: The NAD relays credentials and the server decides. A challenge is how a second factor is requested through AAA.

questions.question: R1 has the configuration below and the TACACS+ server at 10.10.99.20 is up. Admin logs in over SSH using the local account's password, which differs from admin's password on the TACACS+ server. What happens?
questions.code:
aaa new-model
!
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.10.99.20
 key T@cKey!2024
!
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
!
username admin privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Adm1n!9
choices: R1 tries TACACS+, then local, and admin logs in
The server rejects the password and the login fails; the local database is not tried
R1 uses the local account first because local is the most secure method
The login succeeds at privilege level 1
questions.explanation: IOS moves to the next method only when a method fails to answer. The server answered with a reject, so the login fails even though the local password would have matched.

questions.question: Type the global command that turns on AAA on a Cisco router or switch.
questions.explanation: aaa new-model enables AAA and switches logins to method lists. Create a local user first, because remote logins then check the local database by default.
